text: Reading Passage 3 has six sections, A-F.
Choose the correct heading for sections A-D from the list of headings below.

list: Reasons for the increased rate of bullying
Research into how common bullying is in British schools
The reaction from schools to enquiries about bullying
The effect of bullying on the children involved
Developments that have led to a new approach by schools

items.title: A recent survey found that in British secondary schools
options: there was more bullying than had previously been the case.
there was less bullying than in primary schools.
cases of persistent bullying were very common.
indirect forms of bullying were particularly difficult to deal with.

items.title: Children who are bullied
options: are twice as likely to commit suicide as the average person.
find it more difficult to relate to adults
are less likely to be violent in later life.
may have difficulty forming relationships in later life.

items.title: The writer thinks that the declaration 'There is no bullying at this school'
options: is no longer true in many schools.
was not in fact made by many schools.
reflected the school's lack of concern.
reflected a lack of knowledge and resources.

items.title: What were the findings of research carried out in Norway?
options: Bullying declined by 50% after an anti-bullying campaign.
Twenty-one schools reduced bullying as a result of an anti-bullying campaign.
Two years is the optimum length for an anti-bullying campaign.
Bullying is a less serious problem in Norway than in the UK.

items: The most important step is for the school authorities to produce a <input> which makes the school's attitude towards bullying quite clear. It should include detailed <input> as to how the school and its staff will react if bullying occurs.

In addition, action can be taken through the <input>. This is particularly useful in the early part of the process, as a way of raising awareness and encouraging discussion. On its own, however, it is insufficient to bring about a permanent solution.

Effective work can also be done with individual pupils and small groups. For example, potential <input> of bullying can be trained to be more self-confident. Or again, in dealing with group bullying, a 'no blame' approach, which avoids confronting the offender too directly, is often effective.
Playground supervision will be more effective if members of staff are trained to recognise the difference between bullying and mere <input>.
body.title: What steps should schools take to reduce bullying?

items.title: Which of the following is the most suitable title for Reading Passage 3?
options: Bullying: what parents can do
Bullying: are the media to blame?
Bullying: the link with academic failure
Bullying: from crisis management to prevention
